claim: Neurogenesis is the generation of neurons from stem cells, a process that is regulated by SoxB transcription factors (TFs) in many animals.
source: Neurogenesis is the generation of neurons from stem cells, a process that is regulated by SoxB transcription factors (TFs) in many animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other scholarly work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: SoxB transcription factors are central players in neurogenesis across a broad range of animal taxa including vertebrates, insects, nematodes, planarians, and cnidarians.
source: SoxB transcription factors (TFs) are central players in neurogenesis across a broad range of animal taxa including vertebrates, insects, nematodes, planarians, and cnidarians (Alqadah et al., 2015; Meulemans and Bronner-Fraser, 2007; Richards and Rentzsch, 2015; Ross et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Vertebrate SoxB TFs are commonly subdivided into the SoxB1 group (Sox1, Sox2, and Sox3) that maintain stemness in neural stem cells, while SoxB2 group members (Sox14 and Sox21) are involved in neural differentiation.
source: Vertebrate SoxB TFs are commonly subdivided into the SoxB1 group (Sox1, Sox2, and Sox3) that maintain stemness in neural stem cells, while SoxB2 group members (Sox14 and Sox21) are involved in neural differentiation (Bylund et al., 2003; Holmberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on vertebrate SoxB genes.

claim: Vertebrate SoxB genes act sequentially in neurogenesis.
source: Hence, vertebrate SoxB genes act sequentially in neurogenesis, but it is unclear whether this feature is ancestral or derived in metazoan animals.
evidence: This claim is based on the previously cited literature about vertebrate SoxB function.

claim: A similar SoxB subdivision has not been observed in invertebrates.
source: Furthermore, SOX orthology has been notoriously hard to interpret and, therefore, a similar SoxB subdivision has not been observed in invertebrates (Flici et al., 2017; Jager et al., 2011; Richards and Rentzsch, 2015; Schnitzler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on invertebrate SoxB genes.

claim: Cnidarians are the sister group to bilaterians.
source: Cnidarians are the sister group to bilaterians (Kayal et al., 2018; Zapata et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Multiple SoxB genes are expressed in the developing nervous systems of representatives of the two main cnidarian clades, Anthozoa and Medusozoa.
source: As in vertebrates, multiple SoxB genes are expressed in the developing nervous systems of representatives of the two main cnidarian clades, Anthozoa (corals and sea anemones) (Magie et al., 2005; Richards and Rentzsch, 2014; Richards and Rentzsch, 2015) and Medusozoa (hydroids and jellies) (Flici et al., 2017; Jager et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on cnidarian SoxB expression.

claim: Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus is a colonial hydrozoan cnidarian.
source: Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus is a colonial hydrozoan cnidarian (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Frank et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to a figure showing the organism.

claim: Hydractinia possesses a population of stem cells, known as i-cells, that self-renew and contribute to somatic lineages, including neurons, and to germ cells throughout life.
source: like other hydrozoans, this animal possesses a population of stem cells, known as i-cells. These i-cells self-renew and contribute to somatic lineages, including neurons, and to germ cells throughout life (DuBuc et al., 2020; Gahan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on Hydractinia i-cells.

claim: i-cells first appear in embryonic endoderm.
source: i-cells first appear in embryonic endoderm (Gahan et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: i-cells migrate to the outer tissue layer of the body, the epidermis, during metamorphosis.
source: but migrate to the outer tissue layer of the body, the epidermis, during metamorphosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), remaining there during adult life.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a figure showing i-cell migration.

claim: In the mature animal, undifferentiated i-cells are found in interstitial spaces of the epidermis, primarily of the lower body column.
source: In the mature animal, undifferentiated i-cells are found in interstitial spaces of the epidermis, primarily of the lower body column.
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about the location of i-cells in adult animals.

claim: i-cells differentiate while migrating orally.
source: They differentiate while migrating orally (Bradshaw et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: i-cells give rise to various cell types including the two main neuronal lineages: neurons and nematocytes.
source: They differentiate while migrating orally (Bradshaw et al., 2015), giving rise to various cell types including the two main neuronal lineages: neurons and nematocytes
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and describes the differentiation potential of i-cells.

claim: Nematocytes are specialized stinging cells that are used by cnidarians to capture prey or for defence from predators.
source: nematocytes − the latter being specialized stinging cells that are used by cnidarians to capture prey or for defence from predators.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about nematocyte function.

claim: The Hydractinia nervous system has a typical cnidarian nerve-net structure with a higher concentration of neurons at its oral end.
source: The Hydractinia nervous system has a typical cnidarian nerve-net structure with a higher concentration of neurons at its oral end (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to figures showing the nervous system structure.

claim: The Hydractinia genome encodes three SoxB-like genes (Soxb1, Soxb2, and Soxb3).
source: The Hydractinia genome encodes three SoxB-like genes (Soxb1, Soxb2, and Soxb3) whose orthologous relation to specific bilaterian homologs cannot be resolved due to low sequence conservation.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic content of Hydractinia.

claim: The orthologous relation of Hydractinia SoxB genes to specific bilaterian homologs cannot be resolved due to low sequence conservation.
source: The Hydractinia genome encodes three SoxB-like genes (Soxb1, Soxb2, and Soxb3) whose orthologous relation to specific bilaterian homologs cannot be resolved due to low sequence conservation.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and phylogenetic inference.

claim: Hydractinia Soxb2 is expressed in proliferative, putative neural progenitors.
source: A previous study has shown that Hydractinia Soxb2 is expressed in proliferative, putative neural progenitors, and Soxb3 is expressed in neural cells, identified by their distinctive morphology.
evidence: This claim is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Hydractinia Soxb3 is expressed in neural cells, identified by their distinctive morphology.
source: A previous study has shown that Hydractinia Soxb2 is expressed in proliferative, putative neural progenitors, and Soxb3 is expressed in neural cells, identified by their distinctive morphology.
evidence: This claim is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Soxb2 and Soxb3 are essential for adult neurogenesis and nematogenesis in Hydractinia.
source: Both genes are essential for adult neurogenesis and nematogenesis (Flici and Frank, 2018; Flici et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The functions of Soxb1, Soxb2, and Soxb3 in embryonic neurogenesis remain unknown.
source: However, the functions of Soxb1, Soxb2, and Soxb3 in embryonic neurogenesis remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: In sexual polyps, Soxb1 was expressed in cells morphologically resembling i-cells and germ cells in males and females.
source: In sexual polyps, Soxb1 was expressed in cells morphologically resembling i-cells and germ cells in males and females (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In feeding polyps, Soxb1 was expressed in cells that resembled i-cells both with respect to their morphology and their anatomical location, being primarily distributed in the lower body column of the polyp and largely absent from the oral end of the animal.
source: In feeding polyps, Soxb1 was expressed in cells that resembled i-cells both with respect to their morphology and their anatomical location, being primarily distributed in the lower body column of the polyp and largely absent from the oral end of the animal (Bradshaw et al., 2015; Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1 and a citation.

claim: All Soxb1+ cells also expressed Piwi1 and vice versa.
source: We found that all Soxb1+ cells also expressed Piwi1 and vice versa (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Soxb1 is expressed in i-cells, that is, in stem cells that give rise to somatic cells (including neurons and nematocytes) and to germ cells.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Soxb1 is expressed in i-cells, that is, in stem cells that give rise to somatic cells (including neurons and nematocytes) and to germ cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH data showing co-expression of Soxb1 and Piwi1.

claim: Soxb2 expression partially overlapped with Soxb1 in the mid-region of the polyp body column, being largely absent from the lower (aboral) area of the polyp that primarily included only Piwi1+/Soxb1+ cells.
source: Soxb2 expression partially overlapped with Soxb1 in the mid-region of the polyp body column, being largely absent from the lower (aboral) area of the polyp that primarily included only Piwi1+/Soxb1+ cells (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Soxb3 was expressed in the middle and upper (i.e., oral) parts of the polyp and partly overlapped with Soxb2 in the mid-region.
source: Soxb3 was expressed in the middle and upper (i.e., oral) parts of the polyp and partly overlapped with Soxb2 in the mid-region (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Soxb1 promoter-driven tdTomato was not only observed in stem/progenitor cells but was present in neural cells as well, based on the distinct morphology of these cells.
source: Contrary to the mRNA FISH data (Figure 1), the Soxb1 promoter-driven tdTomato was not only observed in stem/progenitor cells but was present in neural cells as well, based on the distinct morphology of these cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Soxb1::tdTomato transgenic reporter shown in Figure 3.

claim: In sexual polyps, tdTomato was also observed in maturing germ cells.
source: In sexual polyps, tdTomato was also observed in maturing germ cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Soxb1::tdTomato transgenic reporter shown in Figure 3.

claim: Soxb1+ cells differentiated into neural cells and gametes.
source: This shows that Soxb1+ cells differentiated into neural cells and gametes as expected.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of tdTomato in neural cells and gametes in the Soxb1 reporter.

claim: The Soxb2 promoter-driven GFP was visible in neurons and nematocytes but not in i-cells.
source: The Soxb2 promoter-driven GFP was visible in neurons and nematocytes but not in i-cells (Figures 2 and 3F–I)
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Soxb2::GFP transgenic reporter shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Soxb2+ cells were more committed than i-cells (i.e., Soxb1+ cells).
source: suggesting that Soxb2+ cells were more committed than i-cells (i.e., Soxb1+ cells).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Soxb2 is not expressed in i-cells but in their progeny.

claim: The spatial distribution of Soxb1+ and Soxb2+ cells was distinct from that of their respective progeny, consistent with migrating neural progenitors that differentiate during and following their migration away from the lower body column area where i-cells and their early progeny reside.
source: The spatial distribution of Soxb1+ and Soxb2+ cells was distinct from that of their respective progeny, consistent with migrating neural progenitors that differentiate during and following their migration away from the lower body column area where i-cells and their early progeny reside.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial expression patterns observed in the transgenic reporters.

claim: The Rfamide reporter was only visible in sensory and ganglionic neurons.
source: The Rfamide reporter was only visible in sensory and ganglionic neurons (Figure 3J–L), consistent with the expression pattern of this gene in neurons but not in neural progenitors (Gahan et al., 2017; Kanska and Frank, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Rfamide::GFP transgenic reporter shown in Figure 3 and citations.

claim: tdTomato-positive (i.e., Soxb1+), GFP-low or negative (i.e., Soxb2-) cells transformed to double positive cells.
source: We observed tdTomato-positive (i.e., Soxb1+), GFP-low or negative (i.e., Soxb2-) cells transforming to double positive cells (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo time lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mRNA expression data and live imaging of transgenic reporter animals are consistent with sequential expression of SoxB genes in the neural lineage.
source: Collectively, our mRNA expression data and the ones obtained previously (Flici et al., 2017) together with the results of our live imaging of transgenic reporter animals are consistent with sequential expression of SoxB genes in the neural lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including FISH and live imaging.

claim: Piwi1+ (i.e., Soxb1+ i-cells) represent approximately 1.4% of the live single-cell population of the Soxb2::GFP transgenic animal.
source: Piwi1+ (i.e., Soxb1+ i-cells) are known to represent a rare population, representing approximately 1.4% of the live single-cell population of the Soxb2::GFP transgenic animal (DuBuc et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Soxb2+ cells (i.e., putative neural progenitors) were an equally rare population.
source: We found that Soxb2+ cells (i.e., putative neural progenitors) were an equally rare population (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rfamide+ neurons were distributed among two distinct populations that differed in levels of GFP expression, accounting for 1.6% and 1.8% of the live single cells, respectively.
source: Rfamide+ neurons were distributed among two distinct populations that differed in levels of GFP expression, accounting for 1.6% and 1.8% of the live single cells, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The brightest Piwi1::GFP cells were small with a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, consistent with stem cell morphology.
source: Imaging flow cytometry of the Piwi1::GFP reporter animal (i.e., cells that also express Soxb1) revealed that the brightest cells were small with a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, consistent with stem cell morphology (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Piwi1+ cells were almost exclusively in S/G2/M phase.
source: Flow cytometric cell cycle analysis (Figure 5G–L) revealed that the Piwi1+ cells were almost exclusively in S/G2/M phase (Figure 5G), similar to what has been observed in i-cells from the freshwater polyp Hydra (Buzgariu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5 and a citation.

claim: i-cell progeny, defined by low GFP fluorescence and constituting a highly heterogeneous population, were found in all stages of the cell cycle.
source: However, i-cell progeny, defined by low GFP fluorescence and constituting a highly heterogeneous population, were found in all stages of the cell cycle (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Soxb2+ cells that include putative neural progenitors had a cell cycle profile similar to i-cells, mostly found during the S/G2/M phases of the cell cycle.
source: Soxb2+ cells that include putative neural progenitors (Flici et al., 2017) had a cell cycle profile similar to i-cells, mostly found during the S/G2/M phases of the cell cycle (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5 and a citation.

claim: Rfamidehigh and Rfamidelow neurons that are thought to be terminally differentiated were mostly in G0/G1, similar to what was observed in nematocytes.
source: Rfamidehigh and Rfamidelow neurons that are thought to be terminally differentiated were mostly in G0/G1, similar to what was observed in nematocytes (Figure 5I and K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The two RFamide+ neuronal populations are probably different, as the RFamide neuropeptide is considered a marker for differentiated neurons.
source: The two RFamide+ neuronal populations are probably different, as the RFamide neuropeptide is considered a marker for differentiated neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of RFamide as a neuronal marker.

claim: Typical neuronal genes were expressed by RFamide+ cells.
source: Indeed, typical neuronal genes were expressed by these cells (Figure 5M; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5M and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The RFamide+ neurons fraction also expressed minicollagen genes that are markers of nematogenesis.
source: The RFamide+ neurons fraction also expressed minicollagen genes that are markers of nematogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on transcriptomic analysis of sorted RFamide+ cells.

claim: Co-expression of minicollagens and precursors of neuropeptides has been reported previously.
source: Co-expression of minicollagens and precursors of neuropeptides has been reported previously (Sunagar et al., 2018; Wolenski et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: A droplet microfluidic single-cell handling system (InDrop) was used to generate a single-cell transcriptome dataset based on 7071 cells from Hydractinia wild type feeding polyps.
source: To provide further insight into the composition of the neural cells population, we used a droplet microfluidic single-cell handling system (InDrop) (Klein et al., 2015) to generate a single-cell transcriptome dataset based on 7071 cells from Hydractinia wild type feeding polyps.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: 22 cell clusters were identified from the single-cell transcriptome dataset.
source: This allowed us to identify 22 cell clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A) and their associated upregulated marker genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Putative i-cells, nematoblasts, gland cells, neurons, and a group of mixed progenitors were identified from the single-cell transcriptome dataset.
source: However, we were able to identify putative i-cells, nematoblasts, gland cells, neurons, and a group of mixed progenitors.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the single-cell transcriptome data.

claim: Both Soxb1 and Soxb2 are expressed in a subset of i-cells; presumably in transition to become Soxb2-positive progenitor cells.
source: We find that both soxB1 and soxB2 are expressed in a subset of i-cells; presumably in transition to become soxB2-positive progenitor cells (clusters 13 and 14 in A)
evidence: This claim is based on single-cell transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Soxb3 is only expressed in few cells in cluster 18.
source: while soxB3 is only expressed in few cells in cluster 18 (see A and D).
evidence: This claim is based on single-cell transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Subpopulations of neural cells in H. symbiolongicarpus transition from a soxB2/RFamide low state (cluster 14) that express a G-protein coupled receptor for glutamate to a soxB2/RFamide high state (cluster 13), of which some eventually become soxB2-negative while still expressing high levels of RFamide (cluster 11).
source: It also appears that subpopulations of neural cells in H. symbiolongicarpus transition from a soxB2/RFamide low state (cluster 14) that express a G-protein coupled receptor for glutamate (see E) to a soxB2/RFamide high state (cluster 13), of which some eventually become soxB2-negative while still expressing high levels of RFamide (cluster 11); presumably as terminally differentiated axonal neurons as determined by the markers Kaptin and Contactin2, which are important in synapse and axon formation, maintenance and function (see E).
evidence: This claim is based on single-cell transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hydractinia can regenerate a decapitated head that includes a fully functional nervous system within 2–3 days.
source: Hydractinia can regenerate a decapitated head that includes a fully functional nervous system within 2–3 days (Bradshaw et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Intact animals showed a well-developed head nervous system but had neither S-phase cells nor i-cells in their heads.
source: We also analysed intact animals that showed a well-developed head nervous system but had neither S-phase cells nor i-cells in their heads (Figure 6A), as expected (Bradshaw et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and a citation.

claim: At 12 hpd, there were many cycling cells in the stump area, few neurons (likely remnants of the amputated tissue), and few migrating Piwi2low cells that are probably i-cell progeny.
source: At 12 hpd, there were many cycling cells in the stump area, few neurons (likely remnants of the amputated tissue), and few migrating Piwi2low cells that are probably i-cell progeny (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At 24 hpd, a clear proliferative blastema had been established at the oral most pole, with i-cells (Piwi2high) and their progeny being numerous in the area. However, only a few RFamide+ neurons were visible.
source: At 24 hpd, a clear proliferative blastema had been established at the oral most pole, with i-cells (Piwi2high) and their progeny being numerous in the area. However, only a few RFamide+ neurons were visible (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At 36 hpd, new neurons were visible in the regenerating head and proliferative i-cells and progeny were still present.
source: At 36 hpd, new neurons were visible in the regenerating head and proliferative i-cells and progeny were still present (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At 48 hpd, a nearly complete head nervous system had been established and the regenerating head contained lower numbers of i-cells and progeny.
source: Finally, at 48 hpd, a nearly complete head nervous system had been established and the regenerating head contained lower numbers of i-cells and progeny (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Piwi2low cells, which are presumably i-cell progeny, were the first to migrate to the injury area, followed later on by Piwi2high cells, which are probably stem cells.
source: Hence, Piwi2low cells, which are presumably i-cell progeny, were the first to migrate to the injury area, followed later on by Piwi2high cells, which are probably stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal dynamics of cell populations during regeneration.

claim: This is similar to what has been observed in planarian head regeneration, where neoblast progeny arrive in the injury area before neoblasts.
source: This is similar to what has been observed in planarian head regeneration, where neoblast progeny arrive in the injury area before neoblasts (Abnave et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research on planarian regeneration.

claim: None of the existing neurons incorporated EdU during regeneration, consistent with neurons being terminally differentiated.
source: Of note, none of the existing neurons incorporated EdU during regeneration, consistent with neurons being terminally differentiated.
evidence: This claim is based on EdU incorporation data during regeneration.

claim: In all cases, the neurons remained stationary and did not proliferate during the observation period while a new head nervous system regenerated.
source: In all cases, the neurons remained stationary and did not proliferate during the observation period while a new head nervous system regenerated (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo time lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar to Hydra, head nervous system regeneration in Hydractinia involves de novo neurogenesis rather than proliferation or migration of existing neurons.
source: Hence, similar to Hydra (Miljkovic-Licina et al., 2007), head nervous system regeneration in Hydractinia involves de novo neurogenesis rather than proliferation or migration of existing neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regeneration data and comparison to Hydra.

claim: Soxb1 knockdown affected many aspects of larval development.
source: Soxb1 knockdown affected many aspects of larval development.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the effects of Soxb1 knockdown.

claim: Animals with Soxb1 knockdown were on average smaller and underdeveloped.
source: First, the animals were on average smaller and underdeveloped (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Animals with Soxb1 knockdown had fewer Piwi1+ i-cells and numbers of neurons and nematoblasts was lower than normal. RFamide neuron numbers were low or absent altogether.
source: Second, these animals had fewer Piwi1+ i-cells and numbers of neurons and nematoblasts was lower than normal. RFamide neuron numbers were low or absent altogether (Figure 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Larvae with Soxb1 knockdown had defects in ciliation.
source: Third, these larvae had defects in ciliation (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: As a result of ciliation defects, the movement of larvae with Soxb1 knockdown was restricted.
source: and, as a result, their movement was restricted (larvae swim by coordinated cilia beat).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed ciliation defects.

claim: Larvae with Soxb1 knockdown had lost their ability to metamorphose upon CsCl treatment.
source: Finally, the larvae had lost their ability to metamorphose upon CsCl treatment (Figure 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The loss of metamorphosis ability in Soxb1 knockdown larvae is probably the result of a loss of neurons expressing GLWamide, the internal regulator of metamorphosis in Hydractinia.
source: with the latter probably being the result of a loss of neurons expressing GLWamide, the internal regulator of metamorphosis in Hydractinia (Gajewski et al., 1996; Müller and Leitz, 2002; Schmich et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of GLWamide in metamorphosis and citations.

claim: The number of S-phase cells was upregulated in Soxb1 knockdown larvae compared with the control and proliferative cells were also detectable in the epidermis; normally, S-phase cells are restricted to the gastrodermis in larvae.
source: However, the number of S-phase cells was upregulated compared with the control and proliferative cells were also detectable in the epidermis; normally, S-phase cells are restricted to the gastrodermis in larvae (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Loss of Soxb1 may have resulted i-cells exiting the stem cell program, as observed by Piwi1 staining.
source: Loss of Soxb1 may have resulted i-cells exiting the stem cell program, as observed by Piwi1 staining (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed reduction in Piwi1+ cells.

claim: The increased number of S-phase cells in Soxb1 knockdown could reflect a compensatory response to loss of i-cells or be a response of i-cells to loss of stemness.
source: The increased number of S-phase cells could reflect a compensatory response to loss of i-cells or be a response of i-cells to loss of stemness.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed increase in S-phase cells.

claim: Downregulation of Soxb2 had no visible effect on i-cells or on GLWamide+ neurons.
source: Downregulation of Soxb2 had no visible effect on i-cells or on GLWamide+ neurons (Figure 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: RFamide+ neurons were nearly absent in Soxb2 knockdown embryos.
source: but RFamide+ neurons were nearly absent.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Nematoblast numbers had increased in Soxb2 knockdown embryos and no significant difference was observed on cycling cells.
source: Nematoblast numbers had increased and no significant difference was observed on cycling cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The phenotypes of Soxb2 knockdown in embryos are markedly distinct from what is seen after downregulation of Soxb2 in adult neurogenesis, where the numbers of neurons, nematocytes, and cycling cells are noticeably reduced.
source: These phenotypes are markedly distinct from what is seen after downregulation of Soxb2 in adult neurogenesis, where the numbers of neurons, nematocytes, and cycling cells are noticeably reduced (Flici et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison between embryonic and adult phenotypes with a citation.

claim: The preferential differentiation of neural progenitors to GLWamide+ neurons over RFamide+ neurons in Soxb2 knockdown could be explained by progenitors being limiting, given the essential role of GLWamide+ neurons in metamorphosis.
source: This could be explained by preferential differentiation of neural progenitors to GLWamide+ neurons over RFamide+ neurons if progenitors are limiting, given the essential role of the latter in metamorphosis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed phenotype.

claim: Alternatively, the SoxB2 protein might be maternally loaded or dispensable for embryonic GLWamide+ neurons.
source: Alternatively, the SoxB2 protein might be maternally loaded or dispensable for embryonic GLWamide+ neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed phenotype.

claim: The increase in nematoblast numbers following Soxb2 downregulation could indicate a nematogenesis-inhibiting role for this gene.
source: The increase in nematoblast numbers following Soxb2 downregulation could indicate a nematogenesis-inhibiting role for this gene.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increase in nematoblasts.

claim: Downregulation of Soxb3 had no major effect on the animals, in contrast to the role of this gene in adult neurogenesis.
source: Surprisingly, downregulation of Soxb3 had no major effect on the animals, in contrast to the role of this gene in adult neurogenesis (Flici et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and a citation.

claim: The data suggest an essential and complex role of Soxb2 for embryonic neurogenesis, but also highlight major differences between embryonic and adult neurogenesis.
source: The above data suggest an essential and complex role of Soxb2 for embryonic neurogenesis, but also highlight major differences between embryonic and adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the knockdown experiments.

claim: The requirement for more than one SoxB gene to generate neurons in animals as distantly related as Hydractinia, Drosophila, and mice suggest that more than one SoxB gene had already been present before the cnidarian-bilaterian split to generate neurons in their last common ancestor.
source: However, the requirement for more than one SoxB gene to generate neurons in animals as distantly related as Hydractinia, Drosophila, and mice suggest that more than one SoxB gene had already been present before the cnidarian-bilaterian split to generate neurons in their last common ancestor
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on comparative data across taxa.

claim: Soxb1 is an i-cell marker and probably fulfills a role in stemness.
source: Soxb1 is an i-cell marker and probably fulfills a role in stemness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression and knockdown data.

claim: Soxb1 downregulation resulted in loss of i-cells and impacted other aspects of development including the ability to metamorphose.
source: Its downregulation resulted in loss of i-cells and impacted other aspects of development including the ability to metamorphose, which was expected given that i-cells provide progenitors to multiple lineages.
evidence: This is a summary of the Soxb1 knockdown phenotype.

claim: The function of Soxb1 is similar to the role of vertebrate Sox2.
source: This function of Soxb1 is similar to the role of vertebrate Sox2.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between Hydractinia Soxb1 and vertebrate Sox2.

claim: There is no direct evidence so far to support a similar function of Soxb1 in neural stem cells as vertebrate Sox2.
source: However, vertebrate Sox2 also acts in neural stem cells while in Hydractinia, there is no direct evidence so far to support a similar function.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of evidence for a specific function.

claim: A population of long-term, self-renewing neural progenitors has yet to be identified in cnidarians.
source: Furthermore, a population of long-term, self-renewing neural progenitors has yet to be identified in cnidarians.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Results from Hydractinia, along with data obtained from other cnidarians, are consistent with continuous generation of neurons from multi- or pluripotent cells that also contribute to non-neural lineages, without the existence of a long-term, self-renewing neural stem cell.
source: Our results from Hydractinia, along with data obtained from other cnidarians (reviewed by Rentzsch et al., 2017), are also consistent with continuous generation of neurons from multi- or pluripotent cells that also contribute to non-neural lineages, without the existence of a long-term, self-renewing neural stem cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and comparison to other cnidarians with a citation.

claim: Soxb2 was expressed in a population of cells with uncommitted morphology that differentiated to neural cells, based on GFP retention in neurons and nematocytes in the Soxb2 reporter animal.
source: Soxb2 was expressed in a population of cells with uncommitted morphology that differentiated to neural cells, based on GFP retention in neurons and nematocytes in the Soxb2 reporter animal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Soxb2 reporter data.

claim: In vivo analysis of Soxb1/Soxb2 double transgenic reporter animals has shown that Soxb1+ cells transform into Soxb2+ cells.
source: Our in vivo analysis of Soxb1/Soxb2 double transgenic reporter animals has shown that Soxb1+ cells transform into Soxb2+ cells (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo time lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Downregulation of Soxb2 resulted in neural-specific defects in embryos, consistent with this gene being expressed preferentially in the neural lineage.
source: Downregulation of Soxb2 resulted in neural-specific defects in embryos, consistent with this gene being expressed preferentially in the neural lineage (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Soxb2 knockdown data and expression data.

claim: The neural transcriptional fingerprint and single-cell transcriptomic profiles of Soxb2+ cells support that Soxb2 is expressed preferentially in the neural lineage.
source: The latter is also supported by the neural transcriptional fingerprint (Figure 5M; Supplementary file 2) and single-cell transcriptomic profiles of Soxb2+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5M, Supplementary file 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Deviation from normal development following Soxb2 perturbation was not a simple reduction in all neural cells, as seen in adults.
source: Of note, deviation from normal development following Soxb2 perturbation was not a simple reduction in all neural cells, as seen in adults (Flici et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison between embryonic and adult phenotypes with a citation.

claim: Soxb2 downregulation caused a loss of RFamide+ neurons but not of GLWamide+ neurons.
source: Instead, Soxb2 downregulation caused a loss of RFamide+ neurons but not of GLWamide+ neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: It is possible that the animals preferentially generate GLWamide+ neurons when progenitors are limited because GLWamide+ neurons are essential for metamorphosis of Hydractinia larvae.
source: Because GLWamide+ neurons are essential for metamorphosis of Hydractinia larvae (Plickert et al., 2003), it is possible that the animals preferentially generate this type of neuron when progenitors are limited.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed phenotype with a citation.

claim: Nematoblast numbers increased upon Soxb2 downregulation, suggesting that Soxb2 normally inhibits nematogenesis in embryos, in contrast to its function in adults.
source: Conversely, nematoblast numbers increased upon Soxb2 downregulation, suggesting that Soxb2 normally inhibits nematogenesis in embryos, in contrast to its function in adults (Flici et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increase in nematoblasts with a citation.

claim: Despite being expressed in embryos and larvae, no visible phenotype was observed following Soxb3 downregulation, other than the effect of its downregulation in adults.
source: Despite being expressed in embryos and larvae (Flici et al., 2017), no visible phenotype was observed following Soxb3 downregulation, other than the effect of its downregulation in adults (Flici et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and citations.

claim: Soxb3 may not play a distinct role in embryonic neurogenesis, or that the effect of its downregulation in embryos is too subtle to be observed by our methods.
source: Therefore, Soxb3 may not play a distinct role in embryonic neurogenesis, or that the effect of its downregulation in embryos is too subtle to be observed by our methods.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of observed phenotype.

claim: i-Cells are concentrated in the lower body column.
source: i-Cells are concentrated in the lower body column (Bradshaw et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Neural progenitors are scattered in the mid-body column.
source: neural progenitors are scattered in the mid-body column
evidence: This is a descriptive claim based on the expression patterns observed.

claim: Most neurons and nematocytes are found in the head.
source: while most neurons and nematocytes are found in the head.
evidence: This is a descriptive claim based on the distribution of differentiated cells.

claim: Neural cells differentiate while migrating from the base of the polyp toward the head, reflected by the partly overlapping expression domains of SoxB genes that mark the stages of differentiation.
source: This implies that neural cells differentiate while migrating from the base of the polyp toward the head, reflected by the partly overlapping expression domains of SoxB genes that mark the stages of differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial expression patterns of SoxB genes.

claim: A major question emanating from this work is whether migration is required for neurogenesis cell autonomously, or whether migrating stem cells become exposed to different microenvironments along the oral-aboral axis that drive their differentiation non-cell autonomously.
source: A major question emanating from this work is whether migration is required for neurogenesis cell autonomously, or whether migrating stem cells become exposed to different microenvironments along the oral-aboral axis that drive their differentiation non-cell autonomously.
evidence: This is a statement of an open question arising from the study.

claim: The requirement for multiple SoxB genes and migration seem to be common hallmarks of neurogenesis in all studied animals.
source: However, the requirement for multiple SoxB genes and migration seem to be common hallmarks of neurogenesis in all studied animals.
evidence: This is a general statement based on comparative analysis across taxa.

claim: Hydractinia's continuous, predictable, and accessible neurogenesis across all life stages provides an excellent model to address questions about the evolution and mechanisms of neurogenesis.
source: Hydractinia's continuous, predictable, and accessible neurogenesis across all life stages provides an excellent model to address these questions.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of Hydractinia as a model system.
